Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence in Athens (basis of Year Established): the page states Athens 'is known to have been home to a Jewish community from the second century BCE' (citing C. K. Barrett's commentary on Acts); 2nd c. BCE dated to midpoint -150, c. Presence of a community, no size given. Context not counted as Athens presence: the Moschos son of Moschion 'Ioudaios' manumission/dedication (IJO I Ach45, c. 300-250 BCE) is from the Amphiareion at Oropos, not Athens; the Athenian decree honouring the high priest Hyrcanus (Josephus Ant. 14.149-155; Hyrcanus I c. 106/5 BCE or Hyrcanus II c. 47 BCE) and Athenian honours for Herod and Berenice attest diplomatic relations, not Jewish residents. The same page notes the Agora menorah plaque and possible synagogue date to the 4th-5th c. CE (outside the period).

Encyclopaedia Judaica: 'Concrete information about a Jewish community in Athens is available only from the beginning of the first century C.E.' (dated c. 10 CE as beginning of 1st c. CE). Cites Attic inscriptions naming Jews (IG II2 12609) including one Jerusalemite (IG II2 8934) - undated in the source - and Samaritan epitaphs (IG II2 10219-22; Samaritans not counted as Jews). No figure given. EJ dates the Athenian decree for Hyrcanus (Jos. Ant. 14.149ff.) to Hyrcanus I, 106/5 BCE, as diplomatic relations, not residents.

Philo, Legatio ad Gaium 281 (letter of Agrippa I to Gaius, c. 40 CE): Jerusalem sent colonies 'into Europe, into Thessaly, and Boeotia, and Macedonia, and Aetolia, and Attica, and Argos, and Corinth'. Regional attestation of Jews in Attica (the territory of Athens), not a statement specific to the city; ancient literary source, no figure.

Acts 17:16-17: in Athens Paul 'argued in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons' (Gentile God-fearers). Acts gives no date; c. 50 CE per the conventional dating of Paul's second journey (the Wikipedia Agora-synagogue page gives 54 CE). Indicates an organized community with a synagogue; size unknown.
